Title: Mitigating the Environmental Impact of High-Performance Computing Data Centers

9 
Mitigating the Environmental Impact of High-Performance 
Computing Data Centers 
Zhaojie Lu, Rhibull Tang, Zijia Wan, Zetao Ye 
Shenzhen Middle School, Shenzhen, Guangdong, 518000, China 
Abstract. While High Performance Computing (HPC) is critical for scientific breakthroughs and AI 
development, its growing energy use (often dependent on fossil fuels) requires a detailed 
environmental impact analysis. This study addresses the ever-increasing ecological challenges 
posed by high-performance computing (HPC) data centers by developing a model to quantify and 
predict their energy consumption and carbon emissions. Our model estimates the annual energy 
consumption of HPC data centers globally using data on the size and capacity of small and massive 
data centers. It distinguishes between theoretical maximum and actual energy consumption based 
on average utilization. The results show an upward trend in carbon emissions associated with HPC, 
which are projected to reach 5.81 x 1017 grams of carbon dioxide by 2030. As a result, we propose 
a series of recommendations to reduce the environmental impact of HPC at both the technical and 
policy levels in favor of promoting a healthy and sustainable environment. 
Keywords: High-Powered Computing; Data Center; Electricity Consumption; Generalized Linear 
Model; Polynomial Regression. 
1. Introduction 
High-performance computing (HPC) is a cluster of computers utilizing high-performance 
processors to solve large-scale scientific problems and process massive amounts of data. Due to its 
wide range of applications and efficient computational speed, it plays an increasingly important role 
in finance, government informatization, education, enterprise, and online games. However, at the 
same time, its high energy consumption characteristics seriously impact the environment. In recent 
years, the environmental impact of high-performance computing (HPC) has gradually received 
attention from researchers. Since the high-power input of HPC is usually provided by non-renewable 
energy sources, most commonly fossil fuels, carbon emissions are generated during the combustion 
process, which leads to climate warming. In addition, HPC systems consume large quantities of water 
and chemical coolants, contributing to wastewater pollution. In addition to water pollution, 
components often need to be promptly replaced due to component aging, which tends to generate 
large amounts of e-waste, further exacerbated by the manufacturing process. In addition, the real 
estate construction of data centers and the associated dust and air pollution from power plants 
contribute to the environmental legacy of HPC. The impact of data center ground usage on local 
populations and air pollution from power plants on human health are also among the common HPC 
environmental impacts. Modeling these ecological threats is therefore critical to creating sustainable 
‘green’ HPC solutions in the future. 
If sustainable and inclusive artificial intelligence and other computationally demanding new 
technologies must be developed and manufactured, the environmental impact of high-performance 
computing must be considered. This study combines energy consumption predictions with carbon 
emission factors for various energy sources, including coal, natural gas, renewable energy, and 
nuclear energy. Models are used to quantify and predict the energy consumption and carbon emissions 
of High-Performance Computing (HPC) data centers. An ARIMA model predicts data center 
expansion up to 2030 and assesses the impact on future energy use. The results of the projections can 
be used to make valuable recommendations for energy use and environmental sustainability in the 
current world, contributing to the achievement of the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

2. Problem Restatement 
As HPC hardware in data centers accelerates technological progress, it imposes a heavy 
environmental price. This paper aims to build a model to determine and predict the ecological 
consequences of expanding HPC-based data centers. The model will: 
(1) Estimate the environmental impacts of data center power consumption in terms of annual 
electricity use at full and average operational loads while considering carbon output. 
(2) Project the environmental impacts to 2030, including predicted increases in HPC hardware 
adoption. 
(3) Discuss the implications of the shift toward alternative energy sources and the environmental 
consequences of cooling systems (both sources of emissions and those of waste), respectively. 
(4) Illustrate how the model can capture the positive effect of current and future mitigation 
measures to ease the environmental load of data center infrastructure. 
The work will produce an advisory report to be submitted to the UN Advisory Board, which will 
suggest that the model's results be included in their report on the environmental impact of HPC 
leveraged for AI computation.

It is not feasible to entirely switch to 100% renewable energy; there are a couple of potential 
challenges below: 
(a) Reliability 
(1) Solar and wind power are inherently intermittent, meaning their output fluctuates with 
weather conditions. However, this variation is a significant issue regarding grid stability 
since supply is always required to equalize demand. 
(2) Large-scale energy storage solutions (e.g., batteries, pumped hydro, compressed air) are 
needed to address intermittency and ensure a reliable power supply when renewable 
sources are unavailable. These technologies are still developing and can be expensive. 
(3) Sophisticated grid management, including grid and smart grids, is needed to achieve real-
time supply and demand balance, incorporate heterogeneous renewables, and account for 
variability. 
(b) Infrastructure and Land Use 
(1) Substantial investments are needed to modernize and expand transmission infrastructure to 
bring remote renewable energy generation (e.g., offshore wind farms and solar farms in 
desert regions) to urban areas. 
(2) Renewable energy installations consume large land parcels, affecting ecosystems, 
agriculture, and surrounding communities. Careful site planning and location are critical to 
keep environmental impacts minimal. 
(3) Renewable energy technologies involve significant raw materials (i.e., rare earth minerals 
and silicon). Sustainably and ethically sourcing these materials is an issue that is becoming 
increasingly important. 
(c) Economic and Financial Considerations 
(1) Upfront costs: Moving to 100% renewables requires significant upfront capital 
expenditures to build the new generation capacity, energy storage, and grid capability. 
(2) Shifting away from fossil fuels can lead to job losses in traditional energy industries. New 
jobs and retraining are needed in renewable energy as part of a just transition. 
(3) Affordable energy prices during the transition are essential for equal access to clean energy. 
(d) Social and Political Factors 
(1) Public acceptance: Obtaining public support for large-scale renewable energy installations 
is difficult, mainly because of concerns about aesthetic implications, impacts on land use, 
and environmental consequences. 
(2) Stable and supportive government regulations, policies, and incentives are essential to 
stimulating investment in renewable energy and smoothing the transition. 
(3) The shift towards renewables can alter geopolitical power relations, especially for nations 
whose economy is based on fossil fuel exports. International cooperation is needed to 
manage this transition effectively. 
(e) Technological Development 
(1) Technological developments in energy storage, smart grids, and grid management facilities 
are needed to overcome intermittency and enhance grid reliability. 
(2) Further development of new ‐ generation renewable energy resources (e.g., high ‐
temperature geothermal energy, wave, tidal energy) may extend the renewable energy 
portfolio and decrease the dependence on current‐generation energy resources. 
4. Model Sharing and Response 
4.1 Actionable Recommendations 
4.1.1 Technical Solutions 
(a) Optimize Hardware and Software 


17 
(1) Prioritize the procurement of hardware with high performance-per-watt metrics, such as 
ARM-based processors or specialized accelerators designed for energy efficiency. 
(2) Design and implement energy-efficient algorithms and software. Encourage code profiling 
and optimization practices among HPC users. 
(b) Improve Data Center Efficiency 
(1) Develop advanced cooling systems (e.g., liquid, free-air, evaporative cooling) to decrease 
the energy needed for temperature control. 
(2) Investigate the possibility of collecting and using waste heat produced by HPC systems for 
building heating or other applications. 
(3) Where available, HPC data centers should be powered with renewable energy (solar, wind, 
or hydropower). On-site generation or Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) can be valuable 
tools. 
(c) Promote Green HPC Practices 
(1) Optimize job scheduling algorithms to maximize resource utilization and minimize idle 
time, reducing energy consumption. 
(2) Utilize virtualization and cloud-based high-performance computing (HPC) resources to 
consolidate workloads and optimize resource utilization, eliminating the need for dedicated 
hardware. 
(3) Develop energy-aware workload management systems focusing on energy efficiency 
during job scheduling and running. 
4.1.2 Policy-Oriented Solutions 
(a) Incentivize Green HPC Procurement 
(1) Authorize or encourage energy-efficient HPC hardware and software procurement at 
government-funded research centers and agencies. 
(2) Provide tax relief or financial incentives to organizations seeking green HPC technologies 
and practices. 
(b) Promote Research and Development 
(1) Further, provide government funding to develop energy-efficient HPC hardware, software, 
and data center technologies. 
(2) Foster cooperation to speed up the development and implementation of green HPC 
approaches. 
(c) Establish Energy Efficiency Standards 
(1) Develop standardized metrics and rating systems for evaluating the energy efficiency of 
HPC systems and data centers. Energy Star for HPC could be explored. 
(2) Implement mandatory energy efficiency goals for HPC sites, encouraging operators to 
adopt best practices. 
(d) Raise Awareness and Education 
(1) Provide education courses for HPC users and operators on energy-optimal techniques and 
hardware. 
(2) Present and disseminate green HPC research and best practices through workshops, 
conferences, and web resources. 
(e) International Collaboration: 
Embrace international teamwork for green HPC research, development, and policy to speed 
progress and share expertise globally. 


18 
4.2 Model Response 
When one of the recommendations is acted upon, i.e., when the portion of renewable energy 
increases by 5% from the current 8.5% of all electricity generation worldwide, the carbon emission 
per unit of electricity generation would reduce from 0.22 pound/kWh to 0.135 pound/kWh, which is 
38.6% reduction in carbon emissions. Considering the vast amount of electricity consumption by the 
HPC data center, there is a significant need to promote the transition to renewable energy to protect 
the environment.   
5. Conclusion 
By combining Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), capacity forecasting, and 
various machine learning models (linear regression, polynomial regression, support vector regression, 
random forests, gradient boosting), this paper investigates capacity forecasting and utilization 
forecasting using daily observations from 2021 to 2023 for five major countries. The study results 
show that the energy consumption of HPC infrastructure will increase significantly based on growing 
capacity and utilization. If left unchecked, this growth path will play a key role in global energy and 
greenhouse gas trade, jeopardizing the achievement of the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs), particularly those related to climate action and responsible lifestyles and production. The 
increasing reliance on HPC for artificial intelligence development, scientific research, and other 
computationally intensive tasks necessitates a proactive and comprehensive strategy to mitigate its 
environmental impact. The current trajectory of HPC energy consumption is unsustainable and 
requires immediate attention. In response, this paper proposes measures such as developing energy 
efficiency standards, integrating renewable energy sources, developing sustainable cooling 
technologies, and international cooperation. By incorporating these recommendations into the 2030 
Development Goals, the United Nations can drive HPC towards a more sustainable model.

Abstract: While High Performance Computing (HPC) is critical for scientific breakthroughs and AI development, its growing energy use (often dependent on fossil fuels) requires a detailed environmental impact analysis. This study addresses the ever-increasing ecological challenges posed by high-performance computing (HPC) data centers by developing a model to quantify and predict their energy consumption and carbon emissions. Our model estimates the annual energy consumption of HPC data centers globally using data on the size and capacity of small and massive data centers. It distinguishes between theoretical maximum and actual energy consumption based on average utilization. The results show an upward trend in carbon emissions associated with HPC, which are projected to reach 5.81 x 1017 grams of carbon dioxide by 2030. As a result, we propose a series of recommendations to reduce the environmental impact of HPC at both the technical and policy levels in favor of promoting a healthy and sustainable environment.
